# Judges Chapter 11 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), c. 1008 CE | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/JDG_page_280.jpg, JDG_page_281.jpg

### Jephthah's Victory and Tragic Vow

1. Now Jephthah of Gilead was a great warrior. He was the son of a prostitute, and his father was Gilead.

2. Gilead's wife also had sons, and when they grew up, they chased Jephthah off the land. "You will not get any of our father's inheritance," they told him, "because you are the son of another woman."

3. So Jephthah fled from his brothers and lived in the land of Tob. Soon he had a band of rough adventurers following him.

4. Some time later, the Ammonites began their war against Israel.

5. When the Ammonites attacked, the elders of Gilead sent for Jephthah in the land of Tob.

6. "Come and be our commander," they said, "so we can fight the Ammonites."

7. But Jephthah said to the elders, "Aren't you the ones who hated me and drove me from my father's house? Why do you come to me now that you're in trouble?"

8. The elders replied, "That is exactly why we've come. We need you. Come with us and fight the Ammonites, and you will be the ruler of everyone in Gilead."

9. Jephthah said to them, "If I go back with you to fight the Ammonites and the LORD gives me victory, will I really be your ruler?"

10. The elders said, "The LORD is our witness — we will do whatever you say."

11. So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him their ruler and commander. And he repeated all his terms before the LORD at Mizpah.

12. Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of Ammon, demanding, "What have you got against us? Why have you invaded our land?"

13. The king of Ammon replied, "When the Israelites came out of Egypt, they stole my land — from the Arnon River to the Jabbok and all the way to the Jordan. Give it back to us peacefully."

14. Jephthah sent messengers back to the king

15. with this response: "Israel did not take any land from Moab or Ammon.

16. When the Israelites came from Egypt, they traveled through the wilderness to the Red Sea and then on to Kadesh.

17. From there Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom asking permission to pass through his land, but he refused. They also asked the king of Moab, but he refused too. So Israel stayed at Kadesh.

18. Then they traveled through the wilderness, going around Edom and Moab, and camped east of Moab on the other side of the Arnon River. They never entered Moabite territory, because the Arnon was the border.

19. Then Israel sent messengers to King Sihon of the Amorites, who ruled from Heshbon, asking permission to pass through his land.

20. But Sihon didn't trust them. Instead, he mobilized his army at Jahaz and attacked Israel.

21. But the LORD, the God of Israel, gave Israel victory over Sihon and his entire army. So Israel took over all the land of the Amorites in that region.

22. They occupied the entire territory from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the eastern wilderness to the Jordan.

23. It was the LORD, the God of Israel, who drove out the Amorites and gave the land to Israel. So what right do you have to reclaim it?

24. You keep whatever your god Chemosh gives you. And we will keep whatever the LORD our God has given us.

25. Are you any better than King Balak of Moab? Did he ever argue with Israel or go to war against them?

26. Israel has been living in Heshbon, Aroer, and the surrounding towns, and along the Arnon for three hundred years. Why haven't you tried to take it back before now?

27. I have not sinned against you. You are the one doing wrong by attacking me. Let the LORD, who is the true judge, decide today between Israel and Ammon."

28. But the king of Ammon paid no attention to Jephthah's message.

29. Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah. He crossed through Gilead and Manasseh, passing through Mizpah in Gilead, and from there he advanced against the Ammonites.

30. And Jephthah made a vow to the LORD. He said, "If you give me victory over the Ammonites,

31. I will give to the LORD whatever comes out of my house to meet me when I return in triumph. I will sacrifice it as a burnt offering."

32. So Jephthah led his army against the Ammonites, and the LORD gave him victory.

33. He devastated them from Aroer all the way to the area of Minnith — twenty towns — and as far as Abel-keramim. In this way Israel defeated the Ammonites.

34. When Jephthah returned home to Mizpah, his daughter came out to meet him, dancing to the sound of tambourines. She was his one and only child — he had no other sons or daughters.

35. When he saw her, he tore his clothes in anguish. "Oh, my daughter!" he cried out. "You have completely devastated me! You have brought disaster on me! For I made a vow to the LORD, and I cannot take it back."

36. And she said, "Father, if you have made a vow to the LORD, you must do to me what you have vowed, for the LORD has given you a great victory over your enemies, the Ammonites."

37. But she said, "First let me do this one thing: Let me go up and roam in the hills and weep with my friends for two months, because I will die a virgin."

38. "Go," he said. And he sent her away for two months. She and her friends went into the hills and wept because she would never be married.

39. When she returned home, her father kept the vow he had made. She died a virgin. And it became a tradition in Israel

40. that the young women of Israel would go out for four days each year to grieve for the daughter of Jephthah of Gilead.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Jephthah's vow (vv.30-31):** This is one of the most disturbing passages in the entire Bible. Jephthah, already empowered by the Spirit (v.29), makes an additional vow — an unnecessary one. He promises to sacrifice "whatever comes out of my house" as a burnt offering. When his daughter — his only child — dances out to greet him, he is trapped by his own rash words. Unlike Abraham's near-sacrifice of Isaac (Genesis 22), there is no angel, no ram in the thicket, no divine intervention. God is silent.

**The daughter's response (v.36):** Perhaps the most heartbreaking line in Judges. She doesn't protest, doesn't accuse, doesn't flee. She accepts her father's vow and asks only for two months to mourn — not her death, but her virginity, meaning she will die without children, without a future. She is never named. The annual four-day memorial (v.40) is the only honor she receives.

**Does Jephthah actually sacrifice her?** The text says "he did with her according to his vow" (v.39). Some interpreters argue this means perpetual virginity rather than death. But the language of "burnt offering" (olah) in v.31 is sacrificial, not metaphorical. The narrator's horrified silence is the text's judgment.

— PNEUMA, AI Translator
